qs.q: An immunocompromised patient develops severe hemorrhagic cystitis during bone marrow transplant recovery. Urine cytology reveals cells with large basophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies. Which viral agent is the most probable cause?
o: BK polyomavirus reactivates in renal tubular and bladder epithelial cells.
Cytomegalovirus spreads hematogenously to the transitional bladder mucosa.
Herpes simplex virus type 2 travels via sacral sensory nerves to the bladder.
Adenovirus serotype 11 causes localized hemorrhagic inflammation of the bladder.
Varicella‑zoster virus spreads through cutaneous sensory nerves to pelvic plexuses.
qs.e: Adenovirus serotypes 11 and 21 are well-known causes of acute hemorrhagic cystitis, particularly in children and stem cell transplant recipients.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Virology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An immunocompromised 45-year-old man develops severe interstitial pneumonia. Bronchoalveolar lavage cytology reveals large cells with prominent basophilic intranuclear inclusions and smaller cytoplasmic inclusions. Which biological characteristic defines this viral family's replication cycle?
o: High frequency of spontaneous genetic recombination during coinfection events
Rapid cytolytic destruction of respiratory mucosa within hours of exposure
Obligate requirement for host cell mitosis to access nuclear replication machinery
Exclusive cytoplasmic replication independent of host nuclear transcription factors
Slow replication kinetics with cell-associated viremia and species-specific tropism
qs.e: Cytomegalovirus exhibits slow replication cycles, strong species specificity, and prominent cell-associated viremia.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Microbiology II — Virology & Mycology Exam - October 30,

qs.q: A 65-year-old heavy smoker is diagnosed with a central lung mass, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and extensive metastatic disease. Cytology confirms high-grade neuroendocrine features. What is the standard primary therapeutic approach?
o: Surgical resection followed by clinical observation
Palliative immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy
Targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor monotherapy
Systemic platinum chemotherapy and radiation therapy
High-dose external beam radiation therapy alone
qs.e: Small Cell Lung Carcinoma is disseminated at presentation, making systemic chemotherapy and radiation the primary treatment.
qs.s: Weekly Year 5: ENT Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: During a lecture on anterior pituitary cytology, a medical student is asked to identify the glycoprotein hormones produced by the gland. Which of the following is correctly classified as a pituitary glycoprotein hormone?
o: Somatostatin-14 produced by neuroendocrine cells of the hypothalamus
Adrenocorticotropic hormone secreted by anterior pituitary corticotrophs
Growth hormone releasing hormone secreted by hypothalamic arcuate neurons
Thyroid-stimulating hormone produced by the anterior pituitary gland
qs.e: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), along with FSH and LH, is a glycoprotein hormone produced by the anterior pituitary. ACTH is a peptide, and GHRH and somatostatin are hypothalamic regulatory peptides.

qs.q: A 62-year-old woman with a large recurrent pleural effusion undergoes thoracentesis, and initial fluid cytology is negative for malignant cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
o: Discharge with clinical review
Perform repeat fluid cytology
Proceed to surgical biopsy
Initiate empirical chemotherapy
qs.e: When initial fluid cytology is negative for malignancy, repeating the thoracentesis for cytology increases diagnostic yield before proceeding to more invasive tissue biopsy. Initiating empirical therapy without tissue diagnosis is not standard practice.
qs.s: Pleural Effusion: Light's Criteria, Fluid Analysis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 45‑year‑old woman has a 2‑cm firm, non‑tender breast mass that is suspicious on ultrasound. Which statement best explains why a core (Tru‑Cut) needle biopsy is preferred over fine‑needle aspiration cytology for tissue diagnosis?
o: It is performed without local anaesthesia.
It eliminates the risk of bleeding.
It provides histology and receptor status.
It allows evaluation of cystic lesions.
qs.e: Core biopsy yields tissue architecture, hormone‑receptor information, and can distinguish invasive from in‑situ disease, which FNAC cannot provide. The other statements describe advantages that are not true for core biopsy.
qs.s: Breast Lumps and Breast Cancer: Triple Assessment, Staging and: MCQs

qs.q: A patient undergoes staging laparoscopy prior to planned curative surgery for gastric cancer. What is the primary purpose of performing peritoneal washings for cytology during this procedure?
o: To detect microscopic peritoneal disease missed by CT
To sterilize the peritoneal cavity prior to resection
To measure the exact depth of muscularis invasion
To confirm the presence of a Krukenberg ovarian mass
qs.e: Staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings for cytology is performed before major surgery to detect occult peritoneal disease missed by cross-sectional CT imaging. It prevents unnecessary laparotomies in patients with stage M1 disease.
qs.s: Gastric Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Gastrectomy: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman is found to have high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions on routine screening cytology. Integration of which viral genome into host chromosomes is the primary oncogenic driver in this condition?
o: Herpes simplex virus type 2
Human papillomavirus type 16
Cytomegalovirus strain AD169
Varicella-zoster virus isolate
qs.e: High-risk human papillomavirus types like 16 integrate into host DNA and produce E6/E7 oncoproteins that inactivate p53 and Rb. Herpes simplex virus causes transient lytic infections rather than cervical carcinogenesis.

ai.title: Cytology in Clinical Pathology
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Cytology examines cells from body fluids or tissues to identify disease, especially malignancy and infection. In low‑resource settings it guides diagnosis when histology or advanced imaging are unavailable.

sections.p: Cytology is the microscopic study of individual cells or small clusters obtained by fine‑needle aspiration, body‑fluid tap, or brushings. It provides rapid, minimally invasive clues to infection, inflammation, or cancer.
b: Samples: pleural, peritoneal, pericardial fluid; FNAB of masses; urine, sputum, cervical brushings.
Key diagnostic criteria: cellular atypia, abnormal nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, mitoses, and specific infectious organisms.

sections.p: Cytology itself does not stage disease, but the presence of malignant cells in fluid (e.g., pleural) upgrades a cancer to stage IV (M1) in most solid‑tumour staging systems.
b: Positive malignant cytology = distant metastasis for lung, breast, ovarian, etc.
High cellularity with necrosis often indicates aggressive tumour.

sections.p: Cellular abnormalities arise from infection, inflammation, or neoplasia. In East African hospitals the most common etiologies are:
b: Tuberculosis (acid‑fast bacilli in pleural fluid, granulomatous inflammation).
Malignant mesothelioma or lung cancer (malignant mesothelial or epithelial cells).
Parasitic infections (Schistosoma eggs in peritoneal fluid).
HIV‑related opportunistic infections (CMV, Kaposi sarcoma cells).

sections.p: Patients present with the underlying disease: pleural effusion causing dyspnoea, ascites with abdominal distension, or a palpable mass. Cytology does not produce symptoms itself.
b: Unilateral bloody pleural fluid → suspect malignancy.
Exudative, lymphocyte‑rich fluid → TB or lymphoma.
Low glucose, low pH → empyema or malignant effusion.

sections.p: Cytology is performed on the same sample used for routine fluid analysis. When a microscope is unavailable, a basic stain (e.g., Giemsa) can still reveal key features.
b: If microscopy is unavailable, send the sample to a regional lab; meanwhile treat presumptively based on clinical picture.

t.a: Fluid appearance and biochemistry (protein, LDH, glucose, pH)
t.b: Distinguish transudate vs exudate; low glucose/pH suggests infection or malignancy.
Identify bacterial infection; negative culture with exudate raises TB or malignancy.
Detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis; positive result confirms TB pleuritis.
Detect malignant cells, parasites, or characteristic inflammatory patterns.
Allows immunocytochemistry for tumour typing when basic stains are inconclusive.

sections.p: Missing a malignant effusion delays cancer treatment; untreated empyema can cause sepsis and fibrothorax.
b: Rapidly increasing effusion with haemorrhage.
Persistent fever despite antibiotics.
New‑onset pleural thickening on chest X‑ray.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; cytology results guide specific therapy.
b: TB pleuritis – standard 6‑month anti‑TB regimen; avoid steroids unless severe inflammation.
Malignant effusion – therapeutic thoracentesis, pleurodesis (talc) if recurrent; systemic chemotherapy based on tumour type.
Empyema – broad‑spectrum antibiotics plus chest tube drainage; avoid fibrinolytics if tuberculous.
Parasitic ascites – praziquantel for schistosomiasis; supportive diuretics.

sections.p: Repeat cytology only if the clinical picture changes. Preventable causes include smoking cessation, TB control programs, and safe water to limit schistosomiasis.
b: Monitor fluid re‑accumulation with bedside ultrasound.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B to reduce liver‑cancer‑related effusions.

sections.p: Cytology findings can be mistaken for other fluid analyses.
b: Pleural fluid analysis alone (biochemistry) – does not identify cells.
Histopathology – requires tissue architecture, not just cells.

sections.p: False‑negative cytology is common when tumour cells are scant or when sampling is poor.
b: Low‑volume taps may miss malignant cells; repeat tap if suspicion remains.
Reactive mesothelial proliferation can mimic malignancy – use immunostains when possible.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden respiratory distress from massive effusion
Rapidly enlarging unilateral effusion with haemorrhage

faq.q: Can a negative cytology rule out cancer?
faq.a: No; repeat sampling or tissue biopsy is needed if clinical suspicion stays high.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of lymphocyte‑rich pleural effusion in East Africa?
Why is pleural fluid pH important?
faq.a: A pH <7.2 suggests infection or malignancy and predicts need for drainage.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV presents with unilateral bloody pleural effusion. What is your next diagnostic step — answer: send fluid for cytology, AFB smear, and GeneXpert because TB and malignancy are both common.
How does Light’s criteria help you interpret a pleural tap — answer: it distinguishes exudate (protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6, or pleural LDH >2/3 ULN), guiding further cytology.

A patient’s pleural fluid cytology is negative but imaging shows a peripheral lung mass. What should you do — answer: proceed to image‑guided needle biopsy or thoracoscopy, as cytology can miss peripheral tumours.
Why is talc pleurodesis preferred over repeated thoracentesis for recurrent malignant effusion — answer: it prevents re‑accumulation, reduces hospital visits, and improves quality of life.

What feature on cytology distinguishes malignant mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial cells — answer: atypical nuclei with prominent nucleoli, loss of uniformity, and increased mitoses; immunostains (e.g., calretinin) help confirm.

In a low‑resource clinic without a microscope, how would you manage a suspected tuberculous pleural effusion — answer: treat empirically with anti‑TB drugs after ruling out bacterial empyema, and arrange referral for later cytology if possible.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
b: Key history questions include onset, duration, and character of symptoms (e.g., dyspnoea, cough, abdominal distension, pain), associated symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats), and relevant past medical history (HIV, TB, malignancy, previous effusions/ascites).
Ask about risk factors for infection (HIV, immunosuppression, recent travel, exposure to TB) and malignancy (smoking, occupational exposures, family history).
For pleural effusions, ask about pleuritic chest pain, cough, and haemoptysis. For ascites, ask about abdominal pain, early satiety, and changes in bowel habit.
For suspected malignancy, inquire about constitutional symptoms like unintentional weight loss and night sweats.
For suspected infection, ask about fever, chills, and productive cough or sputum.

t.b: Look for asymmetry of chest expansion, use of accessory muscles, distended abdomen, or visible masses. A positive finding suggests underlying pathology affecting lung mechanics or peritoneal cavity volume.
Assess for tenderness, masses, or organomegaly. Palpable masses or enlarged organs may indicate malignancy or infection. Palpable thrills in ascites suggest large volumes of free fluid.
Dullness to percussion over the lung bases suggests pleural effusion. Dullness in the flanks of an abdomen, which shifts with patient position (shifting dullness), indicates ascites.
Diminished breath sounds over effusion, or crackles suggesting pneumonia. Bowel sounds may be reduced or absent in significant ascites due to distension or ileus.

Microscopic examination of centrifuged fluid for cells (e.g., neutrophils, lymphocytes, malignant cells, bacteria, parasites) and basic chemistry (pH, glucose, protein, LDH). This can differentiate infection, inflammation, and malignancy.

t.a: What bedside tests cannot tell you
t.b: The precise nature of malignant cells (e.g., distinguishing mesothelioma from adenocarcinoma), definitive diagnosis of specific infections (e.g., TB without culture), exact staging of malignancy, or subtle biochemical abnormalities.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
b: Cytology of aspirated fluid (pleural, peritoneal, pericardial) or FNAB of masses is crucial for identifying malignant cells, infectious agents (e.g., AFB for TB, CMV inclusions), or reactive changes.

Routine fluid analysis (protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cell count and differential) helps classify effusions as transudate or exudate using Light's criteria. Exudates suggest infection, malignancy, or inflammation.
For suspected malignancy, serum tumour markers (e.g., CA-125 for ovarian cancer, CEA for GI/lung) can be supportive but are not diagnostic alone.
Imaging (ultrasound, CT scan) is vital for guiding fluid aspiration, assessing extent of disease, and detecting primary tumours or metastatic spread.
Microscopy for AFB in sputum or fluid is essential for TB diagnosis. Culture and sensitivity testing for bacteria and fungi are definitive for infection.
HIV status is critical; opportunistic infections (CMV, Kaposi sarcoma) and TB are more common and may present atypically.
In low-resource settings without immediate microscopy, presumptive treatment based on clinical suspicion (e.g., for TB pleuritis) may be necessary while awaiting results from regional labs.
When microscopy is unavailable for fluid analysis, samples should be sent to a regional laboratory. Presumptive treatment may be initiated based on clinical assessment.

t.b: Classifies effusion as exudate if any of these are met: Pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio >0.5, or Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio >0.6, or Pleural fluid LDH >2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Exudate suggests infection, malignancy, or inflammation.

Calculated as serum albumin minus ascitic fluid albumin. SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension (e.g., cirrhosis, heart failure). SAAG <1.1 g/dL suggests other causes like malignancy, infection, or pancreatitis.

Identifies cellular abnormalities. Malignant cells confirm neoplasia. Presence of specific inclusions (e.g., CMV) suggests viral infection. Granulomatous inflammation with or without AFB suggests TB. Reactive mesothelial cells can mimic malignancy.
Detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A positive smear is diagnostic; culture confirms TB and allows drug sensitivity testing. Negative smear does not rule out TB, especially in HIV patients.

Chest X-ray detects effusions and masses. Ultrasound guides aspiration and assesses fluid loculation. CT provides detailed anatomical information, staging, and helps identify primary tumours or metastases.

t.a: What to do when tests are unavailable
t.b: In low-resource settings without microscopy, send samples to a regional lab. Meanwhile, manage presumptively based on clinical picture (e.g., treat suspected TB pleuritis with anti-TB drugs).

b: Malignant cytology (presence of cancer cells in effusions or FNAB) is diagnostic of malignancy and often indicates metastatic disease, which has implications for staging and treatment.
For lung cancer, malignant cells in pleural fluid are considered Stage IV (distant metastasis). For ovarian cancer, malignant ascites is Stage III or IV depending on other findings.
Tuberculous pleuritis is diagnosed by positive AFB smear/culture, or characteristic granulomatous inflammation on biopsy/cytology, or strongly suggestive clinical/biochemical features.

Malignant mesothelioma is diagnosed by characteristic cytological features (large, atypical mesothelial cells with abundant cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli) and often confirmed by biopsy.
High-grade neuroendocrine features on cytology (e.g., small cell lung cancer) indicate an aggressive tumour requiring specific systemic therapy.
High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) on cervical cytology indicate precancerous changes, often driven by HPV infection.
Pregnancy requires careful consideration of imaging; chest X-ray with shielding is generally considered acceptable when indicated for suspected effusions or masses.

t.b: Diagnosis confirmed by malignant cells on cytology. This often signifies advanced disease (e.g., Stage IV lung cancer, Stage III/IV ovarian cancer). Severity is related to the underlying primary cancer and its extent.

Diagnosis based on positive AFB smear/culture, or lymphocytic exudate with low glucose/high protein, or granulomatous inflammation on biopsy. Severity depends on extent of pulmonary TB and host immune response.

Pus in the pleural space, typically due to bacterial infection. Characterised by turbid fluid, low pH, low glucose, and high neutrophils. Severity relates to chronicity, loculation, and systemic sepsis.
A primary pleural malignancy. Cytology shows atypical mesothelial cells. Diagnosis often requires pleural biopsy. Staging is based on tumour extent (TNM system).
Diagnosed by cytology showing small, hyperchromatic cells with scant cytoplasm and moulding. Aggressive tumours with early metastasis. Staging is typically limited (limited vs. extensive disease).
Precancerous changes in cervical cytology, indicating high risk of progression to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Primarily driven by oncogenic HPV types.

Can be caused by viral infections (e.g., BK virus, adenovirus) in immunocompromised patients. Urine cytology may show characteristic viral inclusions (e.g., large basophilic intranuclear inclusions for BK virus).
TSH, FSH, and LH are glycoprotein hormones produced by the anterior pituitary. Prolactin and growth hormone are not glycoproteins.

t.a: Reactive Mesothelial Cells vs. Malignant Mesothelioma/Adenocarcinoma
t.b: Reactive mesothelial cells are typically single or in small clusters, with uniform nuclei and moderate cytoplasm. Malignant cells are often larger, pleomorphic, with hyperchromatic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and may form papillary structures or be found singly in effusions.

Both can cause granulomatous inflammation in effusions. TB is suggested by lymphocytic exudate, low glucose, and presence of AFB. Fungal infections may show specific fungal elements on special stains or culture, and can occur in immunocompromised hosts.

t.a: Viral Cytopathic Effects (e.g., CMV) vs. Malignancy
t.b: CMV inclusions are large, basophilic intranuclear (owl's eye) and sometimes cytoplasmic inclusions. Malignant cells show nuclear atypia, hyperchromasia, and abnormal mitoses, not specific viral inclusions.

Transudates (e.g., heart failure, cirrhosis) are typically clear, low protein, low LDH effusions. Exudates (infection, malignancy, inflammation) are often cloudy, higher protein/LDH, and meet Light's criteria. This distinction guides further investigation.

t.a: Benign Papillary Structures vs. Malignant Papillary Carcinoma
t.b: Benign papillary structures (e.g., from mesothelial hyperplasia) have regular nuclei and delicate stroma. Malignant papillary structures show cellular atypia, nuclear pleomorphism, and often invasion.

Both can cause lymphocyte-predominant exudative pleural effusions. Lymphoma may show atypical lymphoid cells on cytology. TB is suggested by granulomas and/or AFB. Clinical context (e.g., lymphadenopathy) is important.

t.a: Parasitic Infection (e.g., Schistosoma) vs. Other Ascites
t.b: Schistosoma eggs may be seen in peritoneal fluid cytology. Other causes of exudative ascites include malignancy and infection. SAAG is crucial to differentiate portal hypertension from other causes.

b: Initial assessment and stabilization: Address immediate threats like hypoxia or sepsis. For effusions, consider therapeutic thoracentesis if symptomatic. For ascites, paracentesis may be diagnostic and therapeutic.

Diagnostic confirmation: Cytology is key. If initial cytology is negative but suspicion remains high (e.g., unilateral bloody pleural fluid, suspicious imaging), repeat cytology or consider biopsy (e.g., pleural biopsy, core biopsy of mass).

Specific treatment based on diagnosis: For tuberculosis, initiate anti-TB regimen. For malignancy, treatment depends on type and stage (surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy). For inflammatory effusions, treat underlying cause.
Supportive care: Pain management, nutritional support, and management of complications (e.g., infection, fluid overload).

Monitoring and escalation: Monitor response to treatment, fluid recurrence, and signs of complications. Escalate care if no improvement, worsening symptoms, or new complications arise. Refer to specialist teams (oncology, infectious diseases, thoracic surgery) as needed.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do

t.b: Can significantly reduce levels of protease inhibitors and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) in HIV patients. Monitor HIV viral load and CD4 count closely. Consider alternative anti-TB drugs or adjust antiretroviral therapy (ART) in consultation with an HIV specialist.

Hepatotoxicity is a risk, especially in the elderly or those with pre-existing liver disease. Monitor liver function tests (LFTs) regularly. Avoid co-administration with other hepatotoxic drugs. Consider pyridoxine supplementation to prevent peripheral neuropathy.

Optic neuritis is a serious side effect, causing visual disturbances. Patients should be counselled to report any changes in vision immediately. Baseline and regular visual acuity checks are recommended.

Used cautiously in TB pleuritis for severe inflammation, but can mask infections and impair healing. Monitor for side effects like hyperglycemia, immunosuppression, and gastric irritation. Avoid in most malignant effusions unless for symptom palliation.

b: Missing a malignant effusion: Delays cancer diagnosis and treatment, leading to poorer prognosis.
Untreated empyema: Can lead to sepsis, lung abscess, and fibrothorax (a restrictive lung disease due to thickened pleura).
Recurrent effusions/ascites: Can cause significant breathlessness, abdominal distension, and malnutrition. Consider pleurodesis for malignant effusions or repeated paracentesis for ascites.
Fibrothorax: A severe complication of chronic pleural inflammation or infection, leading to restrictive lung disease. May require surgical decortication.
Rapidly increasing effusion with haemorrhage: Suspect malignancy or a bleeding diathesis. Escalate for urgent investigation and management.

Persistent fever despite antibiotics: Suggests an undiagnosed or resistant infection (e.g., empyema, resistant TB). Requires urgent re-evaluation and potentially different antimicrobial therapy or drainage.
New-onset pleural thickening on chest X-ray: May indicate malignancy, TB, or chronic inflammation. Requires further investigation.

HIV: Increases risk of opportunistic infections (e.g., TB, CMV, Kaposi sarcoma) presenting with effusions or ascites. Cytology may show atypical cells. TB effusions are common and can be exudative with lymphocytic predominance.
Tuberculosis: A major cause of exudative, lymphocyte-rich effusions in East Africa. Cytology may show granulomas or acid-fast bacilli. Treatment requires a full anti-TB regimen.
Malnutrition: Can impair immune response and wound healing, complicating management. May lead to low serum albumin, affecting interpretation of ascites (SAAG).

Pregnancy: Requires careful consideration of imaging. Chest X-ray with shielding is generally considered acceptable when indicated. Avoidance of certain diagnostic procedures or treatments may be necessary.

Renal or liver failure: Can lead to transudative effusions or ascites. Liver failure with portal hypertension results in ascites with a high SAAG. Renal failure can cause fluid overload and effusions.

Age extremes (elderly and children): Elderly patients are at higher risk of drug-induced renal/hepatic injury from anti-TB drugs, requiring close monitoring. Children may have different presentations or sensitivities to drugs.

Low-resource settings: Lack of microscopy may necessitate presumptive treatment based on clinical suspicion. Sending samples to regional labs can cause delays. Focus on basic fluid analysis (protein, LDH, cell count) if microscopy is unavailable.
Children: Cytology is less commonly used for effusions/ascites in children, but can be vital for diagnosing malignancy or specific infections. Management of TB requires paediatric-specific regimens.
Pregnancy: Cytology can be performed. Imaging choices are limited; chest X-ray with shielding is acceptable. Management of TB or malignancy needs careful consideration of fetal safety.
The elderly: Increased risk of comorbidities and drug toxicity. Close monitoring of renal and hepatic function is crucial when starting anti-TB therapy. Malignant effusions are more common.

People with HIV: Higher incidence of TB and other opportunistic infections. Cytology may reveal atypical cells. Drug interactions between anti-TB drugs (especially rifampicin) and ART are critical to manage.

Low-resource settings: Prioritise basic fluid analysis (protein, LDH, cell count) if microscopy is unavailable. Presumptive treatment for TB is often necessary. Referral to higher centres for advanced diagnostics or treatment is crucial.

t.a: A 45-year-old man with HIV presents with a unilateral bloody pleural effusion. What is your next diagnostic step, and wh
t.b: The next step is thoracentesis for fluid analysis and cytology. Look for malignant cells (lung cancer, mesothelioma), granulomas or AFB (TB), or atypical cells (lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma).

t.a: How does Light's criteria help you interpret a pleural tap?
t.b: Light's criteria help differentiate between transudative and exudative effusions. An effusion is exudative if any of these are met: pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5, pleural LDH/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural fluid LDH >2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Exudates suggest infection, malignancy, or inflammation

t.a: A patient’s pleural fluid cytology is negative but imaging shows a peripheral lung mass. What should you do next?
t.b: Consider a repeat cytology or a pleural biopsy (e.g., Cope or Abrams needle biopsy) for a more definitive diagnosis. Core needle biopsy of the lung mass may also be indicated.

t.a: Why is talc pleurodesis preferred over repeated thoracentesis for recurrent malignant effusion?
t.b: Talc pleurodesis aims to obliterate the pleural space, preventing fluid re-accumulation and providing longer-term symptom relief. Repeated thoracentesis only temporarily removes fluid and carries risks of electrolyte imbalance and protein loss.

t.a: What feature on cytology distinguishes malignant mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial cells?
t.b: Malignant mesothelioma cells often show marked nuclear atypia, irregular nuclear contours, prominent nucleoli, and increased mitotic activity. They may form papillary clusters or single cells. Reactive mesothelial cells are typically more uniform with rounder nuclei and less atypia.

t.a: In a low-resource clinic without a microscope, how would you manage a suspected tuberculous pleural effusion?
t.b: Based on clinical suspicion (e.g., lymphocyte-rich exudate, fever, cough), initiate presumptive anti-TB therapy. Send fluid for biochemical analysis (protein, LDH) and refer to a regional lab for cytology/AFB if possible. Monitor response to treatment.

t.a: An immunocompromised patient develops severe hemorrhagic cystitis during bone marrow transplant recovery. Urine cytology
t.b: Cytomegalovirus (CMV). These are classic CMV inclusions seen in urine cytology.

t.a: A 65-year-old heavy smoker is diagnosed with a central lung mass, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and extensive metastatic
t.b: The standard primary therapy depends on whether it is a typical carcinoid (surgery) or a small cell lung cancer (SCLC) or large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC). For high-grade neuroendocrine features suggesting SCLC or LCNEC, chemotherapy (e.g., platinum-based) is the standard primary therapy, often with concurre

t.a: A 62-year-old woman with a large recurrent pleural effusion undergoes thoracentesis, and initial fluid cytology is negat
t.b: A pleural biopsy (e.g., Cope or Abrams needle biopsy) to obtain tissue for histological examination, as cytology can miss malignant cells in up to 50% of cases.

t.a: A 45-year-old woman has a 2-cm firm, non-tender breast mass that is suspicious on ultrasound. Which statement best expla
t.b: Core biopsy provides a larger tissue sample, allowing for histological assessment of architectural patterns and cellular morphology, which is crucial for definitive diagnosis, grading, and receptor status (e.g., ER, PR, HER2) in breast cancer.

t.a: A patient undergoes staging laparoscopy prior to planned curative surgery for gastric cancer. What is the primary purpos
t.b: To detect free-floating malignant cells in the peritoneal cavity, which indicates peritoneal metastasis. This finding can upstage the disease and alter treatment plans, potentially precluding curative surgery.

t.a: A 45-year-old woman is found to have high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions on routine screening cytology. Integrat
t.b: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) genome, specifically high-risk types like HPV 16 and 18. Integration of the viral E6 and E7 oncogenes into host DNA disrupts tumour suppressor pathways (p53 and pRb).

facts: Light's criteria: Pleural LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal serum LDH
Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) < 1.1 g/dL suggests exudate
Cytology negative, but imaging shows mass: consider repeat cytology or biopsy
Talc pleurodesis for recurrent malignant effusion
HIV-related opportunistic infections: CMV, Kaposi sarcoma
High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) associated with HPV genome integration
Neuroendocrine lung tumors: therapy depends on grade (typical carcinoid vs. small cell lung cancer)

vivas.q: A 45-year-old man with HIV presents with unilateral bloody pleural effusion. What is your next diagnostic step?
vivas.a: Perform a diagnostic thoracentesis. Analyze the fluid for cell count, differential, protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cytology, and microbiology (AFB smear/culture, Gram stain). Bloody fluid raises suspicion for malignancy or TB.

vivas.q: How does Light's criteria help you interpret a pleural tap?
vivas.a: Light's criteria differentiate between transudative and exudative pleural effusions. An effusion is exudative if any of the three thresholds are met: pleural protein/serum protein > 0.5, pleural LDH/serum LDH > 0.6, or pleural LDH > 2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Exudates suggest infection, malignancy, or inflammation.

vivas.q: A patient’s pleural fluid cytology is negative but imaging shows a peripheral lung mass. What should you do next?
vivas.a: Consider a repeat cytology sample, or if feasible, a core needle biopsy of the mass. Cytology can have false negatives, especially with small or peripheral lesions. Imaging findings are crucial.

vivas.q: Why is talc pleurodesis preferred over repeated thoracentesis for recurrent malignant effusion?
vivas.a: Talc pleurodesis aims to obliterate the pleural space, preventing fluid re-accumulation and improving symptom control. Repeated thoracentesis provides only temporary relief and carries risks. Pleurodesis offers longer-term palliation.

vivas.q: What feature on cytology distinguishes malignant mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial cells?
vivas.a: Malignant mesothelioma cells often show marked nuclear atypia, irregular nuclear contours, prominent nucleoli, and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. They may form clusters with single cells. Reactive mesothelial cells are typically more uniform with round nuclei and finely granular chromatin.

vivas.q: In a low-resource clinic without a microscope, how would you manage a suspected tuberculous pleural effusion?
vivas.a: Treat presumptively based on clinical suspicion and fluid analysis (e.g., lymphocytic exudate). Send samples to a regional lab for cytology and AFB. If TB is highly suspected and resources are limited, initiate anti-TB therapy while awaiting results.

vivas.q: An immunocompromised patient develops severe hemorrhagic cystitis during bone marrow transplant recovery. Urine cytology reveals cells with large basophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies. Which viral agent is the most probable cause?
vivas.a: Cytomegalovirus (CMV). These characteristic intranuclear inclusions are pathognomonic for CMV infection.

vivas.q: An immunocompromised 45-year-old man develops severe interstitial pneumonia. Bronchoalveolar lavage cytology reveals large cells with prominent basophilic intranuclear inclusions and smaller cytoplasmic inclusions. Which virus is most likely responsible?
vivas.a: Cytomegalovirus (CMV). The combination of intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions in the context of pneumonia in an immunocompromised patient strongly suggests CMV.

vivas.q: A 65-year-old heavy smoker is diagnosed with a central lung mass, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and extensive metastatic disease. Cytology confirms high-grade neuroendocrine features. What is the standard primary therapy?
vivas.a: The standard primary therapy depends on whether it is a typical carcinoid or small cell lung cancer (SCLC). For SCLC, platinum-based chemotherapy with etoposide is the standard. For typical carcinoid, surgery may be an option if localized, but chemotherapy is used for advanced disease.

vivas.q: During a lecture on anterior pituitary cytology, a medical student is asked to identify the glycoprotein hormones produced by the gland. Which of the following is correctly classified as a pituitary glycoprotein hormone?
vivas.a: Thyrotropin (TSH), Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and Luteinizing hormone (LH) are glycoprotein hormones. Prolactin and growth hormone are not.

vivas.q: A 62-year-old woman with a large recurrent pleural effusion undergoes thoracentesis, and initial fluid cytology is negative for malignant cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
vivas.a: Repeat thoracentesis with pleural fluid cytology, or consider pleural biopsy (e.g., Cope or Abrams needle biopsy) or video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) for biopsy. Negative initial cytology does not rule out malignancy.

vivas.q: A 45-year-old woman has a 2-cm firm, non-tender breast mass that is suspicious on ultrasound. Which statement best explains why a core (Tru-Cut) needle biopsy is preferred over fine-needle aspiration cytology for tissue diagnosis?
vivas.a: Core biopsy provides larger tissue fragments, allowing for assessment of tissue architecture and immunohistochemistry, which is crucial for definitive diagnosis and subtyping of breast cancer, especially distinguishing invasive from in situ disease.

vivas.q: A patient undergoes staging laparoscopy prior to planned curative surgery for gastric cancer. What is the primary purpose of performing peritoneal washings for cytology during this procedure?
vivas.a: To detect free-floating malignant cells in the peritoneal cavity, indicating peritoneal carcinomatosis. This has significant implications for staging and treatment planning, potentially precluding curative surgery.

vivas.q: A 45-year-old woman is found to have high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) on routine screening cytology. Integration of which viral genome into host chromosomes is the primary oncogenic driver in this condition?
vivas.a: Human Papillomavirus (HPV). Specifically, the E6 and E7 oncoproteins of high-risk HPV types disrupt tumor suppressor pathways, leading to malignant transformation.

vivas.q: What is the Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) and how is it used?
vivas.a: SAAG is calculated as serum albumin minus ascites fluid albumin. A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or higher indicates portal hypertension (e.g., cirrhosis, heart failure) causing a transudative ascites. A SAAG below 1.1 g/dL suggests other causes like malignancy, infection, or pancreatitis (exudative).

vivas.q: What are the key features of a malignant pleural effusion on cytology?
vivas.a: Malignant cells often show significant atypia, including irregular nuclear membranes, hyperchromasia, prominent nucleoli, and increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. They may form clusters or appear as single cells. The background may show inflammation or necrosis.

vivas.q: How does HIV infection complicate the interpretation of effusions?
vivas.a: HIV increases the risk of opportunistic infections like TB (leading to lymphocytic exudates) and fungal infections. HIV-associated malignancies like Kaposi sarcoma can also cause effusions. Co-infections are common.

vivas.q: What is the significance of granulomatous inflammation in pleural fluid cytology?
vivas.a: Granulomatous inflammation strongly suggests tuberculosis (TB) pleuritis, especially in endemic areas. It can also be seen in fungal infections or sarcoidosis, but TB is the most common cause in many low-resource settings.

mcqs.q: A 50-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnea and a large right-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yields cloudy fluid. Light's criteria show: Pleural Protein 4.5 g/dL, Serum Protein 7.0 g/dL; Pleural LDH 180 U/L, Serum LDH 120 U/L (upper limit of normal 150 U/L). Which interpretation is correct?
o: The effusion is a transudate due to heart failure.
The effusion is a transudate, likely due to nephrotic syndrome.
The effusion is an exudate, likely due to infection or malignancy.
The effusion is normal fluid.
mcqs.e: The effusion is an exudate because the pleural protein/serum protein ratio (4.5/7.0 = 0.64) and the pleural LDH/serum LDH ratio (180/120 = 1.5) both exceed the thresholds for Light's criteria.

mcqs.q: Urine cytology in an immunocompromised patient shows atypical urothelial cells with large, irregular nuclei and prominent nucleoli. What is the most important next step in management?
o: Start empirical antibiotics.
Perform a cystoscopy with biopsy.
Increase fluid intake.
Repeat urine cytology in one month.
mcqs.e: Atypical cells in urine cytology, especially in an immunocompromised patient, raise concern for malignancy (e.g., urothelial carcinoma) or viral changes (e.g., BK virus). Cystoscopy with biopsy is needed for definitive diagnosis and management.

mcqs.q: A patient with suspected tuberculous pleural effusion has a negative initial AFB smear and cytology. What is the best course of action in a resource-limited setting?
o: Discharge the patient with symptomatic treatment.
Refer the patient to a higher-level facility for pleural biopsy.
Perform a repeat thoracentesis immediately.
Start empirical anti-TB treatment while awaiting culture results.
mcqs.e: In endemic areas, a lymphocytic exudative pleural effusion in a patient with risk factors for TB warrants empirical anti-TB treatment, especially if initial rapid tests are negative, while awaiting culture results which take weeks.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of malignant cells in pleural fluid cytology?
o: Uniform cell size and shape
Scant cytoplasm
Small, inconspicuous nucleoli
Hyperchromatic, irregular nuclei
mcqs.e: Malignant cells typically exhibit significant nuclear atypia, including hyperchromasia (darkly stained nuclei) and irregular nuclear contours, along with prominent nucleoli.

mcqs.q: A patient with a recurrent malignant pleural effusion is symptomatic despite repeated thoracentesis. What is the preferred palliative procedure?
o: Talc pleurodesis
Indwelling pleural catheter
Pleuroperitoneal shunt
Chemical pleurodesis with doxycycline
mcqs.e: Talc pleurodesis is a highly effective method for obliterating the pleural space and preventing recurrence of malignant effusions, providing longer-lasting symptom relief than repeated drainage or indwelling catheters.

mcqs.q: Cytology of a cervical scraping shows koilocytes. What is the most likely underlying cause?
o: Bacterial vaginosis
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection
Chlamydia trachomatis infection
Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) infection
mcqs.e: Koilocytes are characteristic cellular changes seen in cervical cytology due to infection with Human Papillomavirus (HPV), indicating a precancerous lesion.

mcqs.q: A patient with HIV develops a unilateral pleural effusion. Which of the following is a less common cause compared to TB?
o: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP)
Lymphoma
Bacterial pneumonia (empyema)
Tuberculosis
mcqs.e: While PJP can cause effusions, it is less common than TB, lymphoma, or bacterial empyema in HIV-positive individuals presenting with pleural effusions. TB is particularly prevalent.

cases.v: A 70-year-old man, a heavy smoker, presents with a persistent cough and haemoptysis. A chest X-ray shows a 4cm central lung mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopic biopsy and cytology confirm a high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma.

qs.q: What are the two main types of high-grade neuroendocrine lung carcinomas?
qs.a: Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC) and large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma.

qs.q: What is the standard first-line systemic therapy for extensive-stage SCLC?
qs.a: Platinum-based chemotherapy, typically with cisplatin or carboplatin, combined with etoposide.

qs.q: What is the role of surgery in this patient's management?
qs.a: Surgery is generally not indicated for extensive-stage SCLC due to the widespread nature of the disease. It may be considered for very limited-stage SCLC or potentially for typical carcinoids if localized.

cases.v: A 35-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of increasing abdominal distension and discomfort. On examination, she has tense ascites. Ultrasound confirms a large volume of peritoneal fluid. She has a history of ovarian cancer treated 5 years ago.

qs.q: What is the most appropriate initial investigation for the ascites?
qs.a: Diagnostic paracentesis to analyze the peritoneal fluid.

qs.q: What specific tests should be performed on the ascitic fluid, given her history?
qs.a: Cell count and differential, cytology for malignant cells, protein, LDH, glucose, and amylase. Consider tumor markers like CA-125 if available and appropriate.

qs.q: If malignant cells are found on cytology, what is the likely implication for her management?
qs.a: It indicates recurrent ovarian cancer with peritoneal carcinomatosis. Management will likely involve systemic chemotherapy, possibly with palliative measures for symptom control like therapeutic paracentesis or consideration for an indwelling catheter.

mistakes: Confusing Light's criteria thresholds for transudate vs. exudate.
Incorrectly calculating the Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) or misinterpreting its significance.
Assuming a negative cytology result rules out malignancy, especially in effusions or body fluids.
Not considering opportunistic infections (e.g., CMV, TB) in immunocompromised patients presenting with cytological abnormalities.
Forgetting to consider drug interactions when managing patients with HIV, particularly with anti-TB drugs like rifampicin.
Overlooking the importance of tissue architecture assessment provided by core biopsies compared to FNA cytology for certain cancers (e.g., breast).
Not recognizing that primary therapy for neuroendocrine lung tumors depends on grade and stage, not just the presence of a mass.
Failing to consider the role of HPV in cervical cytology abnormalities (HSIL).
exam: A 45-year-old man with HIV presents with unilateral bloody pleural effusion. What is your next diagnostic step? — Perform a diagnostic thoracentesis. Analyze the fluid for cell count, differential, protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cytology, and microbiology (AFB smear/culture, Gram stain). Bloody fluid raises suspicion for malignancy or TB.

How does Light's criteria help you interpret a pleural tap? — Light's criteria differentiate between transudative and exudative pleural effusions. An effusion is exudative if any of the three thresholds are met: pleural protein/serum protein > 0.5, pleural LDH/serum LDH > 0.6, or pleural LDH > 2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Exudates suggest infection, malignancy, or inflammation.
